newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden's Asbrink sees no problems with EU advice.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's Asbrink sees no problems with EU advice.

text.p: Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said on Monday he saw no problems with a European Union recommendation on how the country should reduce its budget deficit.

EU finance ministers adopted recommendations for the 10 EU countries which were judged to have had too big budget deficits in 1996. Sweden was one of few countries which made its recommendation public.
The recommendation said Sweden should seek to eliminate its budget deficit in 1998, which is also the aim of the Social Democratic government.
It urged the government to pursue a "cautious" budget policy in view of uncertainty in budget forecasts.

It also reiterated its recommendation from last year that budget measures should be focused on the expenditure side and that the tax burden on companies and households should be as limited as possible.
Asbrink told journalists the tax ratio as well as public expenditure in relation to gross domestic product was already declining. "So I see no problems with these recommendations," he said.
The tax ratio would decline both in 1997 and 1998 and public expenditure was forecast to fall to below 60 percent in 1999 from a peak of 73 percent in 1993.
The recommendation noted that Sweden aimed to reduce its budget deficit to 2.1 percent this year, well below the three percent limit set by the Maastricht treaty, from 3.6 percent last year.
Only five countries -- Finland, Denmark, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Ireland -- met the Maastricht treaty criteria on public finances last year.
